newsitem.title: CHINA: Europe TV makers seek better access to China.
newsitem.headline: Europe TV makers seek better access to China.

text.p: European television producers are seeking better access to China's booming television market through a visit this week to Beijing by European Commission vice-president Leon Brittan, they said on Tuesday.

Brittan, responsible for relations with Asia, is due to arrive in China on Thursday, accompanied by top executives from 29 major European firms including those in broadcasting, recording and telecommunications, the EU embassy said.

For European television producers attending Shanghai's sixth annual international television festival, one of the key issues Brittan will tackle is how to improve their small share of one of the world's fastest growing markets.

Peter Kraewinkels of the European Association of Television Programme Distributors said he would like to see established a working party between the Chinese and European television industry as a result of Brittan's visit.

The working party could clarify rules and procedures on what kinds of programmes were acceptable to China, encourage co-productions and work toward access for European satellite broadcasters to Chinese cable stations, he said.
Kraewinkels was speaking in a hall crowded with booths where deals to buy and sell programmes were being negotiated between Chinese and foreign television companies.

China's television market is huge. It has 3,000 television stations, a third of them educational channels, a third cable channels and a third broadcast channels, with more than 300 million sets and a penetration rate of more than 90 percent in urban areas.

"Business is very good," said Steven Kwok, marketing manager of ATV Enterprises, which sells programmes made by ATV, one of Hong Kong's main two television stations. "There are more and more channels. Demand cannot meet supply."

Kwok said controls over imported television programmes remained tight, with severe consequences for those who broadcast unapproved material, but added that the video cassette market was hard to control.

An official of one Chinese station said there was a maximum of about 33 percent of airtime for foreign programmes, with stricter standards and time-limits for large television stations than for small ones.

One foreign company representative confirmed that, while the controls were strict on large stations, they were more relaxed for smaller stations, which sometimes broadcast foreign programmes without approval.
"It is difficult for the government to monitor properly. The further from Beijing, the less control there is," he said.
"But this is not mathematics and there is no clear line. The borderlines, on nudity and kissing, are being slowly pushed back to satisfy audiences," he said.
